questions.skill: 'Describe two' means two separate features, each with a supporting detail
questions.prompt: Describe two problems faced by the Weimar Republic in 1923.

answers.text:
The occupation of the Ruhr: in January 1923 French and Belgian troops occupied Germany's main industrial area because Germany had failed to pay reparations. Workers went on strike (passive resistance), damaging the economy.

Hyperinflation: the government printed money to pay the strikers, so prices spiralled. By November 1923 a loaf cost around 200 billion marks and savings became worthless.
answers.explanation: Full marks: two problems (1 each), each supported with accurate, specific detail (1 each). The two paragraphs make it obvious to the examiner where each mark comes from.

answers.text:
Hyperinflation was a problem because prices rose so fast that money became worthless. By November 1923 bread cost 200 billion marks.

There was also the Munich Putsch.
answers.explanation: Three marks. The first problem is identified and supported (2); the second is identified but not described (1). One sentence of detail about the Putsch (Hitler's attempt to seize power in Munich in November 1923) would have earned the fourth mark.

answers.text: There was hyperinflation, the Ruhr was invaded, there was the Munich Putsch and the Spartacist uprising.
answers.explanation: Two marks, one for each of the first two problems identified. Listing more problems doesn't earn more marks, because only two are credited. (The Spartacist uprising was in 1919, not 1923.) Two problems in depth beats four in a list.

answers.text: Germany had lots of problems in 1923 because people were angry about the Treaty of Versailles and things were very bad. The Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919 at the end of the First World War, and Germans called it a 'diktat' because they had no say in it. It was very harsh on Germany. The Weimar Republic was very weak and unpopular, and lots of different groups hated it, so it was a very difficult time for Germany and for the German people.
answers.explanation: One mark at most for a vague reference to discontent. The detail about the Treaty of Versailles is accurate, but it is about 1919, and no specific problem of 1923 is named or described. It is the longest answer here and one of the weakest: history marks reward precise knowledge that answers the question asked.

questions.tip: About 5 minutes. Write two short paragraphs: name the problem, then add a specific fact (date, number or event) that describes it. No need for explanation or judgement.

questions.skill: Explain how each change affected people, rather than just describing Nazi policies
questions.prompt:
In what ways were the lives of women affected by Nazi policies?

Explain your answer.

answers.text:
One way was employment. The Nazis believed women's role was 'Kinder, Küche, Kirche', so women doctors, teachers and civil servants were dismissed from 1933, limiting their independence and income. However, from 1937 labour shortages meant women were encouraged back into work, showing ideology giving way to economic need.

Another way was family life. Marriage loans of 1000 marks, with a quarter written off per child, and the Mother's Cross made motherhood women's main source of status. Some women gained recognition, but their choices were narrowed by state pressure…
answers.explanation: Level 4 (7–8 marks): complex explanation of more than one way (employment, family), each supported with precise knowledge. It explains the effect on women's lives and shows change over time and different experiences. That is what lifts it to the top level.

answers.text:
The Nazis wanted women to stay at home and have children. They gave marriage loans and the Mother's Cross to encourage women to have lots of children. This meant women's lives changed because they were expected to be mothers instead of having careers.

Women were also forced out of jobs like doctors and teachers. This meant they lost their independence and had to rely on their husbands.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (5–6 marks): two developed explanations with supporting knowledge, each linked to how women's lives were affected. To reach Level 4, add more precise detail (dates, figures) and a complexity, for example the policy reversal after 1937.

answers.text: Women were given marriage loans when they got married, which were loans of 1000 marks. There was the Mother's Cross for having children: bronze for 4, silver for 6 and gold for 8. It was given out every year on the birthday of Hitler's mother. Women were not allowed to wear make-up or trousers, and they were not supposed to smoke or dye their hair. Women had to leave their jobs as doctors, teachers and civil servants. There was also the Lebensborn programme, where unmarried women could have children with SS officers. The Nazis said women's role was 'Kinder, Küche, Kirche', which means children, kitchen, church. Later on, in 1937, women were allowed to go back to work because there weren't enough workers.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks): lots of good, accurate knowledge, but it describes policy after policy without explaining how they affected women's lives. A long list of facts stays in Level 2; add 'This meant that…' after each point to turn description into explanation.

answers.text: Women's lives were affected a lot by the Nazis because they had to do what Hitler said and they didn't have many rights.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): a simple, general statement with no specific knowledge. It could apply to anyone in Nazi Germany.

questions.tip: About 10 minutes. Write two or three paragraphs, each starting with a 'way' (work, family, appearance). Support it with a fact, then explain the effect with 'This meant that…'.

questions.skill: Judge usefulness through content, provenance and your own knowledge, all in relation to the enquiry

stimulus.label: Source A
stimulus.caption: A poster published by the Nazi Party in 1934. The caption reads 'The whole people says yes!' It shows a large crowd of cheering men, women and children raising their arms in the Nazi salute beneath a swastika flag.

questions.prompt:
How useful is Source A to a historian studying support for the Nazis in Germany?

Explain your answer using Source A and your contextual knowledge.

answers.text:
Source A is useful for showing how the Nazis wanted support to appear. Its content shows a united crowd of all ages saluting, which reflects the Nazi idea of the Volksgemeinschaft (people's community). Its provenance makes it more useful for studying propaganda than genuine opinion: it was made by the Nazi Party in 1934, the year Hitler became Führer after Hindenburg's death, and the slogan 'The whole people says yes!' was probably linked to the plebiscite that approved this. The Nazis had every reason to exaggerate unity.

My own knowledge shows this was not the whole picture. By 1934 opposition parties were banned, and the Gestapo and concentration camps made dissent dangerous, so apparent support could reflect fear. However, many Germans did genuinely support Hitler because of falling unemployment. So the source is useful, but only as evidence of the image the Nazis created, not of how united Germans really were.
answers.explanation: Level 4 (7–8 marks): complex evaluation of content and provenance together, using precise contextual knowledge to test the source and reach a substantiated judgement about how the source is useful, not simply whether it is.

answers.text: Source A is useful because it shows lots of people supporting the Nazis. They are all doing the salute, which shows they are loyal. However, it is less useful because it is propaganda made by the Nazi Party, so they would want to make it look like everyone supported them. In 1934 Hitler also used terror through the SS and Gestapo, so some people may only have pretended to support him.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (5–6 marks): developed evaluation of content and provenance, with relevant context. It treats 'propaganda' as a reason the source is less useful. At the top level, you'd explain that propaganda is very useful for showing what the Nazis wanted people to believe.

answers.text: Source A is not useful because it is biased. It was made by the Nazis so it is propaganda and it only shows one side.
answers.explanation: Level 2, low (3–4 marks): a simple judgement based on provenance, but 'biased so not useful' is a common trap. All sources are useful for something. It also ignores what the source shows and uses no contextual knowledge.

answers.text: The source shows lots of people doing the Nazi salute. There are men, women and children and there is a big swastika flag. The caption says 'The whole people says yes!'
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): describes the source but never judges its usefulness or brings in knowledge. Describing what you can see is only the first step.

questions.tip: Use content, provenance (who, when, why), and your knowledge. Avoid 'it's biased so it's useless': explain what a biased source is useful for.

questions.skill: Argue both sides, then reach a sustained, justified judgement
questions.prompt:
'The main reason Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933 was the Great Depression.'

How far do you agree with this statement?

Explain your answer.

answers.text:
I largely agree: the Depression was the main reason because it created the conditions that made the other factors matter. After the Wall Street Crash, US loans were recalled and German unemployment reached about 6 million by 1932. Desperate voters turned to extremists: Nazi seats rose from 12 in 1928 to 230 in July 1932, making them the largest party.

However, the Depression alone did not make Hitler Chancellor. The Nazis never won a majority, and their vote fell in November 1932. Hitler was appointed through a deal: von Papen persuaded Hindenburg that Hitler could be controlled, with von Papen as Vice-Chancellor.

Overall, this intrigue was the trigger, but it only happened because the Depression had made the Nazis too big to ignore…
answers.explanation: Level 4 (13–16 marks): a complex explanation of the stated factor and at least one other, with precise supporting evidence, and a sustained judgement that shows how the factors link (the Depression made intrigue possible). The judgement is argued from the first line, not just added at the end.

answers.text:
The Depression was an important reason. After the Wall Street Crash in 1929, unemployment rose to 6 million. People were desperate and voted for the Nazis because Hitler promised 'work and bread'.

Another reason was Nazi propaganda. Goebbels used rallies, posters and radio to spread their message, and Hitler flew around Germany giving speeches.

A third reason was the political deal made by von Papen, who persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler as Chancellor in January 1933.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (9–12 marks): developed explanations of three factors with good knowledge, but no judgement about how far the Depression was the main reason. Without comparing the factors, it can't reach Level 4. Finish with a conclusion that weighs them.

answers.text: I agree. The Depression was the main reason because after the Wall Street Crash unemployment went up to 6 million. People were starving and they lost their jobs and their homes. They blamed the Weimar government and wanted a strong leader, so they voted for Hitler. The Nazis promised to give people jobs. This is why Hitler became Chancellor.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (5–8 marks): a developed explanation of one factor with some support, but it is one-sided. 'How far' requires you to consider other factors (propaganda, the weakness of Weimar, the political deal) before deciding.

answers.text: Hitler was born in Austria in 1889. As a young man he wanted to be an artist and he lived in Vienna, but he was rejected by the art academy twice. He fought in the First World War for Germany and was awarded the Iron Cross, and he was gassed near the end of the war. After the war he joined the German Workers' Party, which became the Nazi Party in 1920, and he soon became its leader because he was a good speaker. In 1923 he tried to seize power in the Munich Putsch but it failed and he went to Landsberg Prison for nine months, where he wrote Mein Kampf. When he came out he reorganised the party and set up the SA and the SS. In 1932 he stood for President against Hindenburg but lost. Then in 1933 he became Chancellor, and in 1934 he became Führer.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–4 marks): a detailed and accurate narrative of Hitler's life, but it doesn't address the Depression or explain why he became Chancellor. Storytelling is the biggest trap in 16-mark questions, and a longer story is still a story.

questions.tip: About 20 minutes. Plan: the given factor, then one or two other factors, then a conclusion. State your judgement in the introduction, and in the conclusion explain why one factor mattered most or how the factors linked. Up to 4 extra marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

questions.skill: Identify a difference in content and explain it using both interpretations

stimulus.label: Interpretation A and Interpretation B
stimulus.caption: Interpretation A: A woman who was a member of the League of German Maidens (the girls' branch of the Hitler Youth), remembering her experiences in 1987. (A practice interpretation written for this app.) / Interpretation B: From a history of Nazi Germany written by a British historian in 2005. (A practice interpretation written for this app.)
stimulus.text:
INTERPRETATION A
I loved the camps. We sang around the fire, went hiking and felt that we were part of something bigger than ourselves. For the first time, girls from rich and poor families were treated the same. Nobody forced me to join; I was proud to wear the uniform.

INTERPRETATION B
Membership of the Hitler Youth became compulsory in 1939, and even before then pressure from schools and employers made refusing difficult. Its activities were designed to produce obedient followers: boys were prepared for war and girls for motherhood. Many young people grew bored of the endless drills, and some joined rebel groups such as the Edelweiss Pirates.

questions.prompt:
How does Interpretation B differ from Interpretation A about the Nazis' youth organisations?

Explain your answer based on what it says in Interpretations A and B.

answers.text: A presents the youth organisations as enjoyable and voluntary: the writer 'loved the camps' and says 'Nobody forced me to join'. B presents them as controlling and compulsory: membership 'became compulsory in 1939' and activities were designed 'to produce obedient followers'. So A sees them as fun and uniting; B as a tool of control.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks): a developed difference in content, supported with detail from both interpretations, and summed up clearly.

answers.text: Interpretation A says the girl enjoyed it but Interpretation B says it was compulsory.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): a simple difference identified, but not explained with supporting detail from both.

answers.text: Interpretation A is written by a woman who was a member of the League of German Maidens, which was the girls' branch of the Hitler Youth, and she is remembering her own experiences in 1987. Interpretation B is by a British historian who wrote a history of Nazi Germany many years later, in 2005. This means the two interpretations were written by very different people at very different times.
answers.explanation: Level 1, low: this is about the authors (provenance), which is the next question. This question is about how the content differs, so all the detail about who wrote them earns almost nothing.

questions.tip: Q1 is about what the interpretations say. Find the main difference, quote both, and sum up the contrast in one sentence. About 5 minutes.

questions.skill: Use provenance (who, when, why) and context to explain the difference

stimulus.label: Interpretation A and Interpretation B
stimulus.caption: Interpretation A: A woman who was a member of the League of German Maidens (the girls' branch of the Hitler Youth), remembering her experiences in 1987. (A practice interpretation written for this app.) / Interpretation B: From a history of Nazi Germany written by a British historian in 2005. (A practice interpretation written for this app.)
stimulus.text:
INTERPRETATION A
I loved the camps. We sang around the fire, went hiking and felt that we were part of something bigger than ourselves. For the first time, girls from rich and poor families were treated the same. Nobody forced me to join; I was proud to wear the uniform.

INTERPRETATION B
Membership of the Hitler Youth became compulsory in 1939, and even before then pressure from schools and employers made refusing difficult. Its activities were designed to produce obedient followers: boys were prepared for war and girls for motherhood. Many young people grew bored of the endless drills, and some joined rebel groups such as the Edelweiss Pirates.

questions.prompt:
Why might the authors of Interpretations A and B have a different interpretation about the Nazis' youth organisations?

Explain your answer using Interpretations A and B and your contextual knowledge.

answers.text: A's author was in the League of German Maidens, so her view rests on positive personal memories and may be nostalgic, recalling camps and friendship rather than political purpose. B's author is a historian writing in 2005 with wider evidence, such as the 1939 law making membership compulsory and groups like the Edelweiss Pirates, so he sees their controlling purpose.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks): developed explanation of the difference using the provenance of both authors, supported by contextual knowledge.

answers.text: The authors of Interpretations A and B have different interpretations because they are different people with different backgrounds. Interpretation A is from someone who was there, so she only knows about her own experience. Interpretation B is by a historian who has studied it. This is why their interpretations about the Nazis' youth organisations are different from each other.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple reasons based on provenance, not developed with context or linked to what each says. The first and last sentences restate the question, so they add length but not development.

answers.text: Interpretation A is biased because she was in the Hitler Youth.
answers.explanation: Level 1, low: 'biased' on its own explains nothing. Say why her position would shape her view, and what the historian's position allows him to see.

questions.tip: Think: who wrote each one, when, and with what purpose or evidence? Link each to the view they give. Avoid just saying 'biased'.

questions.skill: Test both interpretations against your own knowledge before judging

stimulus.label: Interpretation A and Interpretation B
stimulus.caption: Interpretation A: A woman who was a member of the League of German Maidens (the girls' branch of the Hitler Youth), remembering her experiences in 1987. (A practice interpretation written for this app.) / Interpretation B: From a history of Nazi Germany written by a British historian in 2005. (A practice interpretation written for this app.)
stimulus.text:
INTERPRETATION A
I loved the camps. We sang around the fire, went hiking and felt that we were part of something bigger than ourselves. For the first time, girls from rich and poor families were treated the same. Nobody forced me to join; I was proud to wear the uniform.

INTERPRETATION B
Membership of the Hitler Youth became compulsory in 1939, and even before then pressure from schools and employers made refusing difficult. Its activities were designed to produce obedient followers: boys were prepared for war and girls for motherhood. Many young people grew bored of the endless drills, and some joined rebel groups such as the Edelweiss Pirates.

questions.prompt:
Which interpretation gives the more convincing account of the Nazis' youth organisations?

Explain your answer based on your contextual knowledge and what it says in Interpretations A and B.

answers.text:
Interpretation B is more convincing overall. Its claim that membership 'became compulsory in 1939' is accurate, and the idea that activities prepared boys for war and girls for motherhood is supported by the emphasis on drill, sport and 'Kinder, Küche, Kirche'. Its reference to the Edelweiss Pirates reflects real opposition, especially during the war.

However, Interpretation A is convincing about why many young people enjoyed the organisations: camps, hiking and a sense of belonging were genuinely attractive, especially for poorer children. So A is convincing about some young people's experiences, but B is more convincing as an overall account because it explains the Nazis' aims and the pressure to join.
answers.explanation: Level 4 (7–8 marks): complex evaluation of both interpretations, each tested against precise contextual knowledge, leading to a substantiated judgement.

answers.text: I think Interpretation B is more convincing because it's true that the Hitler Youth became compulsory in 1939 and that the Nazis wanted to prepare boys for the army. There were also groups like the Edelweiss Pirates who rebelled. Interpretation A is less convincing because it is only one person's view.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (5–6 marks): developed evaluation of one interpretation with good knowledge. To reach Level 4, test A against knowledge too, rather than dismissing it because it is one person's view.

answers.text: Interpretation B is more convincing because it is written by a historian, and historians know more.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks), low: the judgement is based only on provenance. This question asks you to test the content against your own knowledge.

answers.text: Interpretation A is more convincing because she was actually there, so she saw what the youth organisations were really like with her own eyes. The historian was not there.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): a simple judgement with no knowledge used to test either interpretation. Being there is a point about provenance, not a test of what she says.

questions.tip: About 10 minutes. For each interpretation, use your own knowledge to test what it says, then judge which is more convincing and why.

questions.paper: Paper 2 Section A: Britain: Health and the people
questions.skill: Explain significance in the short term and the long term, with specific evidence
questions.prompt: Explain the significance of penicillin for the development of medicine.

answers.text:
Penicillin was significant as the first effective antibiotic, curing bacterial infections that had killed millions. In the short term, after Fleming's 1928 discovery was developed by Florey and Chain and mass-produced in the USA during the Second World War, it saved thousands of soldiers from infected wounds.

In the long term it began the age of antibiotics: many more were developed, deaths from infections like pneumonia fell dramatically, and surgery became safer. However, overuse has created antibiotic-resistant bacteria, so its significance is still developing.
answers.explanation: Level 4 (7–8 marks): complex explanation of significance over the short and long term, with precise supporting knowledge and a consideration of how significance has changed.

answers.text: Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, but it wasn't developed until Florey and Chain in 1940. It was mass-produced during the Second World War and saved many soldiers. It was significant because it was the first antibiotic and could cure infections.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (5–6 marks): a developed explanation with good knowledge. To reach Level 4, explain the longer-term significance (other antibiotics, safer surgery, resistance).

answers.text: Penicillin was important because it could kill bacteria and cure infections. Lots of people's lives were saved.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks): a simple explanation of significance with little specific knowledge (no names, dates or examples).

answers.text: In 1928 Alexander Fleming was working at St Mary's Hospital in London, growing bacteria called staphylococci on petri dishes. He went away on holiday and left some of the dishes out on his bench. When he came back he noticed that mould had grown on one of the dishes, and that the bacteria around the mould had been killed. The mould was called Penicillium notatum, so he called the substance penicillin. He published an article about it in 1929, but he couldn't make enough pure penicillin to test it properly, so he moved on to other work. It is often said that the discovery was a lucky accident.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): a detailed and accurate story of the discovery, but it never explains the significance: what penicillin changed, in the short or long term. Knowing the story is useful, but 'significance' questions are about impact.

questions.tip: Significance = what difference it made. Cover the short term and the long term, and use specific evidence (names, dates, numbers).

questions.paper: Paper 2 Section A: Britain: Health and the people
questions.skill: Compare both events in every point, explaining why they were similar
questions.prompt:
Compare the responses to the Black Death (1348–49) and the Great Plague (1665).

In what ways were they similar?

Explain your answer with reference to both.

answers.text:
The responses were similar because in both periods people did not know that plague was spread by fleas on rats. In 1348 and 1665 many blamed miasma (bad air), so people carried sweet-smelling herbs or pomanders and lit fires to clean the air. Religion mattered in both: in 1348 flagellants whipped themselves in repentance, and in 1665 people prayed, believing God was punishing sin.

In both outbreaks many who could afford to fled the towns. Even the 1665 orders to shut up infected houses reflected the same limited understanding, because neither period had germ theory.
answers.explanation: Level 4 (7–8 marks): complex explanation of similarities, supported with specific knowledge of both events, and an overall explanation of why the responses were similar.

answers.text: In both the Black Death and the Great Plague people thought it was caused by bad air, so they carried herbs. People also prayed to God in both. Rich people fled from the towns in both plagues.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (5–6 marks), low: several valid similarities for both events. It needs more specific detail, and an explanation of why the responses were similar (no knowledge of germs).

answers.text:
In 1348 the Black Death arrived in England, probably through ports in the south-west. People thought God was angry with them, so some people called flagellants whipped themselves in public to show they were sorry for their sins. Others blamed the positions of the planets or bad air. Lots of villages were abandoned because so many people died.

In 1665 there was the Great Plague in London. The Lord Mayor ordered that houses with plague victims had to be shut up for 40 days, with the people inside, and a red cross was painted on the door with the words 'Lord have mercy upon us'. Watchmen stood outside to stop people leaving, and dead bodies were collected at night and buried in plague pits.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks), low: a lot of accurate knowledge, but each event is described separately and most of the details are differences rather than similarities. The question asks what was similar, so both events need to be linked in every point.

answers.text: Both were plagues and lots of people died. The Black Death killed around a third of the population of England, and the Great Plague killed about 100,000 people in London. Both were terrible events.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): a basic point that doesn't address the responses. The death tolls are accurate, but the question is about how people responded.

questions.tip: Every point should mention both events: 'In both 1348 and 1665…'. Finish with why they were similar (the same lack of scientific understanding).

questions.skill: An inference goes beyond the source; the detail proves it

stimulus.label: Source A
stimulus.caption: From a letter written by a shopkeeper in Munich in November 1923. (A practice source written for this app.)
stimulus.text: Yesterday a customer paid me for a loaf with a basket full of notes, and by the afternoon the same notes would not buy a bread roll. My savings, forty years of work, are worth less than the paper this letter is written on. People say the government has betrayed us, and there is talk in the beer halls of men who promise to set things right.

questions.prompt:
Give two things you can infer from Source A about the effects of hyperinflation.

Complete the table: for each, give (i) what you can infer, and (ii) the details in the source that tell you this.

answers.text:
(i) Hyperinflation wiped out middle-class savings.
Detail: 'My savings, forty years of work, are worth less than the paper…'

(ii) It made people lose faith in the government and turn to extremists.
Detail: 'the government has betrayed us… men who promise to set things right.'
answers.explanation: Full marks: two valid inferences (1 each), each supported by a relevant detail from the source (1 each).

answers.text:
(i) People's savings became worthless.
Detail: 'My savings… are worth less than the paper this letter is written on.'

(ii) People turned against the government.
answers.explanation: Three marks: two valid inferences, but the second has no supporting detail from the source.

answers.text:
(i) Prices rose very quickly.
Detail: 'by the afternoon the same notes would not buy a bread roll.'

(ii) A customer paid with a basket of notes.
Detail: 'Yesterday a customer paid me for a loaf with a basket full of notes', which shows how much money you needed to buy a loaf of bread in Munich in 1923.
answers.explanation: Two marks. The first is a valid inference with support; the second just copies the source. An inference must say something the source suggests but doesn't state. Adding a comment on the quotation doesn't turn the second point into an inference, because it still only repeats what the source says.

answers.text:
(i) The writer was a shopkeeper in Munich.
Detail: the source is a letter from a shopkeeper in Munich.

(ii) The letter was written in 1923, during hyperinflation.
Detail: it was written in November 1923.
answers.explanation: Zero: both points come from the provenance (the caption), not the content, and neither is an inference about the effects of hyperinflation. Setting them out in the table format doesn't help.

questions.tip: Only about 6 minutes. 'I can infer that…' should be your own words; the detail should be a short quotation that proves it.

questions.skill: Explain several causes analytically, going beyond the stimulus points
questions.prompt:
Explain why there was opposition to the Weimar Republic in the years 1919–23.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Treaty of Versailles
• the Kapp Putsch

You must also use information of your own.

answers.text:
One key reason was the Treaty of Versailles. Many Germans saw it as a 'diktat' and blamed the Weimar politicians, the 'November Criminals', for signing it. Losing territory and the army being limited to 100,000 men angered nationalists, which is why right-wing groups tried to overthrow the government in the Kapp Putsch of 1920.

Opposition also came from the left. Communists believed Weimar hadn't gone far enough, leading to the Spartacist Uprising in 1919. Finally, the crisis of 1923 increased opposition: when France occupied the Ruhr and hyperinflation wiped out savings, many blamed the government, which encouraged Hitler's Munich Putsch. Together, these show Weimar was attacked from both sides because it was linked to defeat and economic disaster.
answers.explanation: Level 4 (10–12 marks): an analytical explanation of several causes, clearly linked to opposition, using both stimulus points and precise knowledge of its own (Spartacists, the Ruhr, hyperinflation, the Munich Putsch), with an overall line of reasoning.

answers.text: The Treaty of Versailles caused opposition because Germans thought it was unfair. Germany lost land and had to pay reparations, so people blamed the government. The Kapp Putsch happened in 1920 when the Freikorps tried to take over Berlin because they were angry about the army being reduced. There was also the Spartacist Uprising by communists in 1919.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (7–9 marks): a developed explanation of several causes with good knowledge, including its own. To reach Level 4, analyse how each cause led to opposition and link them together.

answers.text: The Treaty of Versailles made people angry. The Kapp Putsch was when people tried to take over. Hyperinflation made money worthless.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (4–6 marks): relevant points, but little explanation of why they caused opposition, and limited detail.

answers.text: The Weimar Republic had lots of problems and people didn't like it, so they opposed it. It was a new government that was set up after the First World War, when the Kaiser abdicated. It was a democracy, which Germany had never had before, and it had lots of enemies.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–3 marks): a general statement with no specific reason for opposition. The background about the Kaiser is accurate but doesn't explain why people opposed the Republic.

questions.tip: About 15 minutes. Use both stimulus points plus at least one of your own. Start each paragraph with a cause, then explain how it led to opposition.

questions.skill: Judge usefulness through content, provenance and context, for this enquiry

stimulus.label: Sources B and C
stimulus.caption: Source B: a photograph published in a Nazi magazine in 1936. Source C: from an account written in secret by a German schoolteacher in 1938. (Practice sources written for this app.)
stimulus.text:
SOURCE B
[Photograph: rows of smiling Hitler Youth members marching in step, carrying swastika flags, watched by cheering crowds.]

SOURCE C
Boys who miss Hitler Youth meetings are named in front of the class. Many of them are too tired to concentrate on Mondays, because the Saturday marches go on all day. One boy told me he only goes because his father would lose his job if he refused.

questions.prompt:
How useful are Sources B and C for an enquiry into the treatment of young people in Nazi Germany?

Explain your answer, using Sources B and C and your knowledge of the historical context.

answers.text:
Source B is useful for showing how the Nazis wanted young people to be seen: disciplined, happy and united. Published in a Nazi magazine in 1936, it is propaganda, so less useful for real experiences but very useful for the image the regime promoted to win the loyalty of the young.

Source C reveals the pressure behind membership: boys were 'named in front of the class' and one joined only because 'his father would lose his job'. Written in secret, it had no reason to flatter the regime, so it is more reliable about everyday experience. Together they show the gap between propaganda and reality.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (6–8 marks): judgements on the usefulness of both sources, based on content and provenance, and supported by contextual knowledge, with an overall judgement.

answers.text:
Both sources are useful in different ways for an enquiry into the treatment of young people in Nazi Germany.

Source B is useful because it shows Hitler Youth members marching and looking happy. But it is propaganda so it might not be true. Source C is useful because it shows that boys were forced to go to the Hitler Youth and were tired. It was written by a teacher who saw it happen.

Overall, both Source B and Source C are useful for an enquiry into the treatment of young people in Nazi Germany, because they are both about young people in Nazi Germany and they both tell us about the Hitler Youth.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–5 marks): some judgement on both sources using content and provenance, but no contextual knowledge and limited development. The conclusion sounds like a judgement but is circular: the sources are 'useful because they are about the topic'.

answers.text: Source B shows boys marching with flags. Source C says boys were named in front of the class.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): describes the content without judging usefulness.

questions.tip: For each source: what it shows (content), how the provenance affects its usefulness, and your own knowledge to support or challenge it. End with a judgement.

questions.skill: State the main difference in view and support it from both

stimulus.label: Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2
stimulus.caption: Interpretation 1: A woman who was a member of the League of German Maidens (the girls' branch of the Hitler Youth), remembering her experiences in 1987. (A practice interpretation written for this app.) / Interpretation 2: From a history of Nazi Germany written by a British historian in 2005. (A practice interpretation written for this app.)
stimulus.text:
INTERPRETATION 1
I loved the camps. We sang around the fire, went hiking and felt that we were part of something bigger than ourselves. For the first time, girls from rich and poor families were treated the same. Nobody forced me to join; I was proud to wear the uniform.

INTERPRETATION 2
Membership of the Hitler Youth became compulsory in 1939, and even before then pressure from schools and employers made refusing difficult. Its activities were designed to produce obedient followers: boys were prepared for war and girls for motherhood. Many young people grew bored of the endless drills, and some joined rebel groups such as the Edelweiss Pirates.

questions.prompt:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about young people's experiences of the Nazi youth organisations.

What is the main difference between these views?

Explain your answer, using details from both interpretations.

answers.text: The main difference is that Interpretation 1 suggests young people joined willingly and enjoyed it, whereas Interpretation 2 suggests they were pressured or forced: 1 says 'Nobody forced me to join', while 2 says membership 'became compulsory' and pressure 'made refusing difficult'.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks): the main difference is clearly identified and supported with details from both interpretations.

answers.text: Interpretation 1 says the writer loved the camps. Interpretation 2 says it became compulsory in 1939 and many young people got bored.
answers.explanation: Level 2, low: relevant details from both, but the main difference isn't stated as an overall point. Sum up the difference in one clear sentence first.

answers.text: Interpretation 1 is from a woman who was there, because she was a member of the League of German Maidens, and she is remembering her experiences many years later, in 1987. Interpretation 2 is from a British historian, who wrote a history of Nazi Germany in 2005 and so would have studied lots of evidence.
answers.explanation: Level 1: this is all about who wrote the interpretations, not the difference in their views. However much provenance detail you give, this question only rewards the content.

questions.tip: One clear sentence stating the main difference in view, then a detail from each interpretation that shows it.

questions.prompt:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 give different views about young people's experiences of the Nazi youth organisations.

You may use Sources B and C to help explain your answer.

answers.text: They may differ because they are based on different evidence. Interpretation 1 is based on one girl's personal memories of the camps, whereas Interpretation 2 draws on wider evidence, such as the 1939 law and accounts like Source C, which shows boys being pressured because 'his father would lose his job'. Using a source like Source B, which shows smiling marchers, could support a more positive view like Interpretation 1.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (3–4 marks): a valid reason (different sources/evidence), explained and supported using Sources B and C.

answers.text: They are different because one is a personal memory and the other is a historian.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–2 marks): a simple reason, not explained or supported.

answers.text: Because people have different opinions about things, and historians often disagree with each other, so their interpretations are different.
answers.explanation: Zero: too general to explain anything about these interpretations. Saying historians disagree is true of every interpretation, so it explains nothing about these two.

questions.tip: Useful reasons: different sources used, different focus (one person or a whole country), or different weight given to evidence. Explain and support it.

questions.topic: Interpretations: how far do you agree?
questions.skill: Use both interpretations and your own knowledge to reach a sustained judgement

stimulus.label: Interpretation 1 and Interpretation 2
stimulus.caption: Interpretation 1: A woman who was a member of the League of German Maidens (the girls' branch of the Hitler Youth), remembering her experiences in 1987. (A practice interpretation written for this app.) / Interpretation 2: From a history of Nazi Germany written by a British historian in 2005. (A practice interpretation written for this app.)
stimulus.text:
INTERPRETATION 1
I loved the camps. We sang around the fire, went hiking and felt that we were part of something bigger than ourselves. For the first time, girls from rich and poor families were treated the same. Nobody forced me to join; I was proud to wear the uniform.

INTERPRETATION 2
Membership of the Hitler Youth became compulsory in 1939, and even before then pressure from schools and employers made refusing difficult. Its activities were designed to produce obedient followers: boys were prepared for war and girls for motherhood. Many young people grew bored of the endless drills, and some joined rebel groups such as the Edelweiss Pirates.

questions.prompt:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about young people's experiences of the Nazi youth organisations?

Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.

answers.text:
I largely agree with Interpretation 2. Membership did become compulsory in 1939, and even before that pressure was intense: schools rewarded members and employers expected membership, supporting its claim that 'refusing was difficult'. Its view that activities prepared boys for war fits the emphasis on drill, shooting and fitness, while girls were trained for motherhood.

However, Interpretation 1 is also valid. Many young people enjoyed the camps, sport and belonging, especially at first, and poorer children gained opportunities they had never had.

Overall, Interpretation 2 is more convincing as a general account because it explains the Nazis' aims and the growing resistance (the Edelweiss Pirates), but it underestimates the genuine enthusiasm Interpretation 1 shows, particularly before 1939.
answers.explanation: Level 4 (13–16 marks): a sustained, balanced evaluation using both interpretations and precise contextual knowledge, reaching a clearly justified judgement. Up to 4 more marks are available for spelling, punctuation and grammar.

answers.text: I agree with Interpretation 2 because the Hitler Youth did become compulsory in 1939, and boys did military-style training. The Edelweiss Pirates show that not everyone was happy. However, Interpretation 1 shows that some young people enjoyed the camps and hiking, so Interpretation 2 isn't completely right.
answers.explanation: Level 3 (9–12 marks): a developed evaluation using both interpretations and some knowledge, with a judgement. More precise knowledge and a sustained line of argument would reach Level 4.

answers.text:
Interpretation 2 says that the Hitler Youth became compulsory in 1939 and that even before that it was difficult to refuse. It says the activities were designed to make young people obedient, and that boys were prepared for war and girls for being mothers. It also says that many young people got bored of the drills and some joined rebel groups like the Edelweiss Pirates.

Interpretation 1 is from a woman who was in the League of German Maidens. She says she loved the camps, singing around the fire and hiking, and that she felt part of something bigger. She also says rich and poor girls were treated the same and that nobody forced her to join.

So the interpretations are very different. I agree with Interpretation 2 because it is by a historian, and historians study lots of evidence, whereas Interpretation 1 is just one woman's memories.
answers.explanation: Level 2 (5–8 marks): describes both interpretations accurately and at length, but mostly by paraphrasing them. The judgement rests on the author rather than on testing the content with your own knowledge, which is what 'how far do you agree' requires.

answers.text: I agree because the Nazis were bad.
answers.explanation: Level 1 (1–4 marks): an unsupported opinion.

questions.tip: About 20 minutes. Test Interpretation 2 with your knowledge, consider Interpretation 1 as the counter-view, then judge 'how far' in the conclusion.

questions.skill: Explain one clear difference with specific detail from both periods
questions.prompt: Explain one way in which ideas about the causes of disease in the nineteenth century were different from ideas in the fourteenth century.

answers.text: In the fourteenth century disease was blamed on unseen supernatural or natural causes: God's punishment for sin, 'bad air' (miasma) or an imbalance of the Four Humours, as with the Black Death. By the late nineteenth century Pasteur's germ theory (1861) showed that microorganisms cause disease, and Koch identified specific bacteria, such as the cause of tuberculosis. So the cause shifted from God and the humours to identified germs.
answers.explanation: Full marks: a clear difference (1), supported by specific knowledge of the fourteenth century (1) and the nineteenth century (1), with the difference explained (1).

answers.text: Ideas about the causes of disease changed a lot between the fourteenth and the nineteenth centuries, because there were lots of important developments in medicine over those 500 years. In the fourteenth century people thought God caused disease, but in the nineteenth century they knew about germs. This shows that ideas about the causes of disease were very different in the nineteenth century, when medicine had become much more scientific.
answers.explanation: Two marks: a valid difference with simple support, but without specific detail (Pasteur, the humours, the Black Death) it can't be fully developed. The opening and closing sentences restate the question, so they add length without adding specific knowledge.

answers.text: In the nineteenth century Louis Pasteur discovered germ theory in 1861.
answers.explanation: One mark: accurate knowledge of one period only. 'Different from' needs both sides.

questions.tip: Pick ONE difference. State it, give specific evidence from each period, and use a comparison word ('whereas', 'by contrast').

questions.skill: Organise the summary into analytical themes with examples
questions.prompt:
Write a clear and organised summary that analyses the Nazis' methods of controlling the German people in the years 1933–39.

Support your summary with examples.

answers.text:
The Nazis combined terror, propaganda and control of everyday life. Terror was the foundation: the Gestapo, the SS and camps such as Dachau (opened 1933) made opposition dangerous, and after the Night of the Long Knives in 1934 even Nazis knew disloyalty could be fatal.

Propaganda worked alongside terror: Goebbels controlled newspapers, radio and film, and rallies such as Nuremberg created a sense of unity. Organisations such as the Hitler Youth and the German Labour Front controlled everyday life. Together these meant most Germans either supported the regime or felt it too dangerous to resist.
answers.explanation: Top level: a clear, organised summary with analytical themes (terror, propaganda, organisations), specific examples, and an explanation of how the methods worked together.

answers.text: The Nazis controlled people through terror. The Gestapo were secret police and people were sent to concentration camps. They also used propaganda. Goebbels controlled the radio and newspapers. There were also big rallies at Nuremberg.
answers.explanation: Middle level: relevant methods with some examples. It needs more analysis of how each method controlled people and how they worked together.

answers.text: The Nazis controlled the German people in lots of different ways between 1933 and 1939. They were very strict and people had to do what Hitler said or they would be punished. If you said anything bad about Hitler you could get into a lot of trouble, so people were scared. The Nazis also wanted everyone to think the same way as them, so they told people what to think. They controlled what people did at school and at work and in their free time. Young people had to join Nazi groups. People who were against the Nazis were taken away. This meant that the Nazis had a lot of control over the German people and there was not much opposition, so the Nazis stayed in power.
answers.explanation: Lower level: a general summary with almost no specific knowledge: no named organisations, people, events or dates. It sounds organised, but 'told people what to think' and 'were taken away' need to become propaganda, Goebbels, the Gestapo and Dachau.

questions.tip: A summary still needs analysis: group methods into themes, give examples, and explain how each kept control.

questions.skill: Explain each cause and show how causes combined
questions.prompt:
Why did Hitler become Chancellor in January 1933?

Explain your answer.

answers.text:
The Depression created the conditions: unemployment rose to around 6 million, and voters turned to extremists, making the Nazis the largest party in the Reichstag by July 1932. Nazi propaganda exploited this, with Hitler presented as a strong leader offering 'work and bread'.

However, the Nazis never won a majority, and their vote fell in November 1932. The decisive factor was political intrigue: von Papen persuaded President Hindenburg to appoint Hitler Chancellor, believing he could be controlled. So the Depression made Hitler popular, but it was the elite's miscalculation that actually put him in power.
answers.explanation: Top level: several causes explained, supported with precise knowledge, and linked together to show how they combined to produce the outcome.

answers.text: The Depression made lots of people unemployed and they voted for the Nazis. Nazi propaganda was also effective, and Hitler was a good speaker. In the end von Papen and Hindenburg made Hitler Chancellor because they thought they could control him.
answers.explanation: Middle level: several relevant causes with some explanation. More precise detail and links between the causes would reach the top level.

answers.text: Hitler became Chancellor because he was very popular and people liked his speeches. He was a very good speaker and he could make crowds excited, and lots of people came to listen to him. People thought he was a strong leader who would make Germany great again.
answers.explanation: Lower level: one simple cause with no specific detail. The extra sentences develop the same single cause without any specific detail.

questions.tip: Aim for three causes. For each: explain how it helped Hitler, give evidence, then link the causes in a conclusion (conditions + trigger).
